title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
description: The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development."Nature is
body: The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development."Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons.This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project."This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess."We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing."My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection."The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

schema.headline: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth

title: Flintshire: Nurse who stole £750,000 from vulnerable 99-year-old struck off
description: A nurse who stole £750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.Rebecca Lou
body: A nurse who stole £750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care. Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.Evidence presented showed more than £370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with £160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her £400,000 house. The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".She convinced the resident to pay £20,000 for a car and £9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs.Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.Burwood told the tribunal the woman asked her to withdraw cash from her bank account and make donations to charities each week.She claimed the donations, which were between £250 and £500 each time, would usually go towards charities that supported the blind or those with heart issues.Burwood said she would either put the cash in charity pots while she was out and about, or hand donations directly to staff in local charity shops.Her legal representative Victoria Rees said the resident had told her "she didn't want anything to be left by the time she died, as she didn't want the government to have her money", adding Burwood "didn't keep any records of the amount of money she withdrew or the amount of money she donated".The pensioner's bank referred the matter to North Wales Police and the force launched an investigation.The resident's bank account was frozen following concerns about spending, but Burwood attempted to have restrictions lifted and took the resident to a bank branch.Bank staff claimed Burwood was "almost blackmailing" the woman, and told her to ask for the accounts to be unlocked.The panel found Burwood told the woman she would not be able to take her on outings if she could not access her money.The hearing was told the resident later told safeguarding staff she was shocked by the amount of money that had been spent from her account.Another nurse also said they overheard Burwood tell the woman, "I will give you the money back" and "sign here".She reported the conversation as evidence of financial abuse and it was decided Burwood would only make supervised visits to the woman.Burwood claimed she had only been asking the pensioner to "sign a condolence card" and it was "not in relation to signing a document".She claimed the resident's eyesight was "very poor" so she had held the card for her, showed her where she should sign and stopped her from signing over the printed words in the card.Police investigated, but the woman did not want to take further action as she described Burwood as a friend, and believed she had "learned from her mistakes". The panel concluded there had been a significant imbalance of power in the relationship.In its ruling, the panel said Burwood had engaged in a "sustained, calculated course of conduct" and had manipulated the resident for personal gain.It added Burwood had taken advantage of the trust the woman had placed in her and "weaponised" it against her.The panel also found Burwood acted dishonestly by failing to tell her employer she held financial lasting power of attorney for a resident at the care home where she worked.It said her actions amounted to serious misconduct, breached fundamental nursing standards and caused both financial and emotional harm.In its decision, the committee said Burwood's actions were "deplorable" and she was "morally culpable", adding that public confidence in the profession would be undermined if a finding of impairment was not made.The panel determined Burwood's conduct was "morally reprehensible, showed premeditated behaviour and indicated a deep-seated attitudinal problem".It determined her behaviour fell far below the standards expected of a registered nurse.Burwood said she "deeply regretted her actions" adding she "saw the resident as her nanna" as an explanation for why she crossed professional boundaries.The victim has since died, but had only been left with enough money to pay for 23 months of care before the council would have had to step in.James Bradford, operations director at Bryn Yr Haul nursing home, said the team there was "deeply saddened by this incident" and "extend our sincere apologies to everyone affected"."The welfare and safeguarding of our residents remain our absolute priority," he said."We fully support the NMC's decision and, since these events, there have been changes in management, and our safeguarding policies and procedures have been reviewed to ensure the continued safety and wellbeing of everyone in our care."

title: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland
description: UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days. As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at t
body: UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days. As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell.The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021. Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years.It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP.As I wrote a year ago, the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance.  The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK.No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky.And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than £400,000 from the party.Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street.Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been. But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction. For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal. We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out.Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that."I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said."I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people."Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions. Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney.Scotland's first minister has said he wants "much more opportunity for a regional dimension to take forward skills, economic opportunity and planning" and his team acknowledge this vision includes overlaps with the regional combined authorities seen in parts of England, albeit without mayors.It will be intriguing to observe, given the rivalry and grit that exists between Labour and the SNP, how things develop beyond the prime minister's speech.Here in Aberdeen, activists have seized upon the prime minister's reflections on Brexit to argue that if he can revisit the outcome of the referendum in 2016 on the European Union, Scots should be able to revisit the one in 2014 on independence. There have been plenty of mentions too of an exchange in the Commons last month between SNP MP Chris Law and Andy Burnham, when Burnham suggested another Scottish independence referendum could be held, if public opinion showed demand for one.SNP folk think - perhaps hope - this represents the prime minister's authentic view. He and Downing Street have seen sought to squash this idea and he said he wanted to "move on" from a debate about Scottish independence.Privately, senior SNP figures accept the authority to sanction another referendum lies with Westminster and the UK government says no. So, their focus is seeking to steadily build the case for independence in how they choose to govern.Within the party, a new group called, you guessed it, "Independence" has been set up.Speaking at its launch event, the SNP's former Policy Convener Toni Giugliano argued that "countries don't become independent by waiting for permission. They do so when support becomes unstoppable and when a national consensus for change is built". Furthermore, he argued, fundamental questions about what an independent Scotland would look and feel like must be answered now - such as the currency that would be used and how the state pension would work.These are the long term questions.For now, the tussle is more short term, as the SNP ponders when the prime minister might call a general election.Buoyed by its recent victory at Holyrood, the party senses Labour vulnerability in the swathe of seats Labour took from them two years ago.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland

title: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
description: The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.These were not the best of circumstances.Katie Zacharia
body: The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.These were not the best of circumstances.Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.In just five days, she was out – the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered – in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day."Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.Trump may be wondering whether Zacharia "needs" the press secretary job, but presidents – including this one - benefit most from a competent press secretary in times of crisis.And while there may not be an immediate crisis, this White House is certainly facing growing adversity.Across the US, Republican candidates are scrambling to hold on to their seats in the upcoming elections. Some are doing so by distancing themselves from the president and his policies, creating new stresses and faultlines within a party that has for so long been broadly unified behind Trump.Meanwhile, the White House has been beset by a series of controversies – including allegations of corruption that forced the resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and an abrupt reversal of plans to publicly air a military execution in December after widespread bipartisan backlash.A skilled press secretary may have been able to navigate these political landmines while continuing to push out the White House's preferred message in the face of a building media frenzy.Karoline Leavitt, who worked as Trump's press secretary from the start of his second term until she resigned in August a few months after welcoming her second child, proved highly adept at defending the administration from the press room lectern while avoiding stumbles and maintaining a collegial relationship with journalists.Her performance set a high bar for Zacharia, who was a relative novice. It was a mark she failed to reach or even approach, although she never really had much of a chance.The speed at which she failed was astounding, setting a modern record for the shortest-tenured White House press secretary.Zacharia's halting Tuesday press conference performance, combined with those questions about her legal background, essentially sealed her fate.And subsequent press appearances, including a less-than-welcoming interview with conservative pundit Sean Hannity on Thursday – which Trump said he watched – did nothing to change that.As president, Trump has essentially acted as his own press secretary, making major announcements and changing policies from the Oval Office, the White House lawn, airfield tarmacs – wherever he happens to be.Zacharia herself noted this phenomenon prior to being tabbed for the White House job. "President Trump does not need a spokesperson," she posted on X. "He is his own best press secretary."Now, he will have to be.Trump's penchant for speaking off the cuff, however, has made the job a difficult one over the course of his two terms in office.His press secretaries have sometimes had their public statements undermined by presidential pronouncements. At other times, they've been left out of the loop of key decisions.When they have been effective, they have managed to ride the choppier waves while also smoothing relations with the media - providing context for inquisitive journalists and helping tamp down any simmering issues.In comments to Fox News on Friday, Trump said that he is in "no rush" to find a new press secretary. But at such a critical time in his second term, Trump will be without the help that someone like Leavitt offered so consistently.He may come to regret not having it.

schema.headline: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump

title: Off Campus star collaboration 'gave me chills', says Babydoll singer
description: The singer behind the TikTok viral hit Babydoll says collaborating with an Off Campus star was "mind-boggling".Jamie Miller, who is originally from Po
body: The singer behind the TikTok viral hit Babydoll says collaborating with an Off Campus star was "mind-boggling".Jamie Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, was close to calling it quits on his music career at the start of 2026, deciding it was his "last chance", financially and emotionally.But over the summer everything changed when Babydoll caught the attention of people on social media, leading to a viral dance, his first UK top 10 single, and reaching number one in the US iTunes pop chart.When Miller saw a comment from actor Antonio Cipriano, saying he "needed this song", he sent him a message suggesting he feature on a recording – then "panicked" and added "haha, joking"."I'm a fan of Antonio's voice, and I have been a fan for a long time," he said."He messaged back and was like, 'If you're actually not joking, I'd be honoured'."Cipriano headed to Los Angeles, where Miller now lives, and they recorded Babydoll on the day they first met, external."It was the best time ever," said Miller."We're coming up at the same time, he has an amazing career in acting and I feel like the stars aligned even for us to do this and the world is rallying around us as a duo too. The opportunities that we're having right now are incredible."Amazon Prime Video's ice hockey romance series Off Campus – based on a book series by Elle Kennedy - has similarly taken the world by storm this year, ranking as the third most-watched series launch in the platform's history, external.It has raised the profile of numerous artists, with a soundtrack merging old favourites with new music.Asked if he would like to be involved with the series in future, Miller said: "I'm such a fan of the show. I think it's absolutely incredible what they're doing, what Antonio is doing. In any capacity, I would love to. We'll see."On Friday, the original version of Babydoll moved from number three to number two in the official UK charts - beaten only by Taylor Swift's Patient Zero.Miller also recently supported The Jonas Brothers on the US leg of their tour, and said bringing Cipriano out as a guest star at some of the shows was "mind-boggling"."I think the easiest thing about it was we're doing it together, for the first time. It was his first arena, it was my first arena, and I think that's the most amazing situation to be in, because we can lean on each other."Backstage we would say to each other, 'we're so lucky, our lives are not normal, we're going out to play for 20,000 people, what are we doing bro?'. "Introducing him gave me chills because, as well as my dreams coming true right now, his dreams are too.  "It's so nice and needed, to have a friend who can guide you through."At 19, Miller competed in The Voice UK, coming third place with coach Jennifer Hudson.But his love for music first began accidentally, when he took part in a primary school show."If you auditioned for the play, then you got to skip out math class," he recalled."Just to see the reaction from the teachers after they asked me to sing a song, was just absolutely like 'I want to do this, this is actually incredible.'"All my mates were rugby players and football players, whereas I just wanted to do music. After that one audition, I was hooked."Now 29, Miller admits the past couple of years have been "really tough", adding changes in the music industry and in his personal life had left him feeling quite lost."Going into this year was my last chance to try and cut through. This industry is really hard, it's really expensive as well," he said."I think the thing with success, people think you have a lot of money... I didn't really see that side of that. So financially, this year, I couldn't really make it work anymore. I was on my last legs."He continued: "Going into this year, I'd built my career off sad music, and I'm not sad anymore, I'm happy."I think Babydoll maybe brought a bit of light to a world that needed it. I know that sounds really cliché to say, but I do feel that is true, we needed some joy."Miller said the whirlwind nature of Babydoll's success had led to accusations he was an "industry plant" - someone who appears to be self-made, while actually having backing from significant investors or supporters."I wish I was an industry plant, I've done this for nine years," he said with a laugh."At first, I was getting told this was coming across as a gimmick. But that's the thing, I'm not trying to be cool, I'm trying to just have fun."Literally, my mentality was 'if I'm going out, and this is my last chance at music, I'm going out my way.'"Miller said he "never had any social media campaign" planned and it "happened the most organic way possible".As the Babydoll dance took hold of social media, Miller collaborated with an array of stars including actors Jennifer Love Hewitt, Lucy Hale and Julianne Hough, as well as popstar Meghan Trainor."All these incredible people I've been able to do it with, they've said it themselves, they've said 'we needed this song'."From all sides of the world, it's kind of unified people in a way, and it's just a beautiful thing to be a part of something that made someone smile."Miller said he was "proud" of his new music and was excited to share his latest album with the world and to tour it – in particular, he said, to bring it to Wales.But he added the non-stop nature of the past couple of months had been "really hard to process"."It feels like so many life changes are happening around me, but I'm still the same person. It's dystopian, in a way."Especially being from Wales, you don't really see stuff like this happening to people all the time. Tom Jones is absolutely incredible, but I feel like he's really been the one that's flown the flag, and rightfully so."I'm very appreciative for everything that's going on right now, and thank my lucky stars. I just hope I'm doing Wales proud, to be honest."

schema.headline: Off Campus star collaboration 'gave me chills', says Babydoll singer

title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondent Reporting fromnear L
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondent Reporting fromnear Lyman, eastern UkraineA Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September –  and suffered few casualties in return.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warningThe Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.Image caption, Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas regionHe is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front lineAn infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous"."The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unitIn Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation."As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed.""I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present."The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained."This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from dronesAll this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin. Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' Johannes Natland jailed over murder plot
description: A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.Johannes Na
body: A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard. During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday. The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes."You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing.He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country. "You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police.When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed."There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan."We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder."Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway.Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school. He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day".He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis.Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions".The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler.Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself."Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired.He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area.He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing.The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets."You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed."From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room. At his trial, one of Natland's footballer friends recalled him talking about the "Swedish Foxes" and telling him: "I'm going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die."Natland also confided in his girlfriend before leaving for the UK, saying in a message: "I'm going on crazy mission."According to her, he said: "Now I can finally kill someone and it's perfect as I get money to do it. "I can kill someone and life will be wonderful."Giving evidence, Natland said he wanted to look "cool" to his peers but it was just "bravado" and inside he was "terrified".He told jurors: "I wasn't an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn't."Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he would have shot himself in the foot to get out of the "pickle" he was in.Flanagan said: "Natland was clearly being tasked by someone in the Foxtrot Network, an organised criminal group sanctioned by the UK and the US due to its involvement in orchestrating violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime."The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case."However, as recent events have shown, Counter Terrorism Policing will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK."Natland was told he will have to serve at least two thirds of the 20-year sentence behind bars.The Norwegian lawyers acting for the 19-year-old said they would work to have him transferred to Norway to serve his sentence. "Twenty years is a very severe sentence for a boy who was 18 when he was arrested," they said in a statement. "The other young people convicted in the related proceedings in Norway mainly received youth sentences or community sentences. "We will take the time to consider the sentence carefully, together with him, his family and his British legal team."Counter Terrorism Policing said it continued to investigate those suspected of helping Natland obtain firearms and a stolen car.In September 2025, a 27-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and was later released under investigation.Two men, aged 30 and 27, were arrested in Bradford on 20 May on suspicion of handling stolen goods, specifically a car.They were taken into custody before being released on bail.

schema.headline: Norwegian teen 'hitman' Johannes Natland jailed over murder plot

title: Jon Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV tour
description: Jon Rahm will give up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV Golf after reaching a separation agreement that will secure his exit from the league.The leag
body: Jon Rahm will give up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV Golf after reaching a separation agreement that will secure his exit from the league.The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its multibillion-dollar backing.Spaniard Rahm was listed as the organisation's top unsecured creditor when LIV filed for bankruptcy, with $7.4m (£5.5m) owed to him for the rest of the 2026 season alone.ESPN reported he is owed about $100m (£75m), external from the remainder of the $300m, (£222m) contract he signed when he left the PGA Tour for LIV Golf in December 2023.Despite LIV securing a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit to try and move forward with 'LIV 2.0', Rahm has deemed the proposed terms are "unacceptable".Instead, he has waived his entire claim in order to have a "complete economic walk-away".However, he will take the rights to 'Legion XIII' - the name of the LIV team Rahm captained - although he will not be allowed to use it to make a team in TGL - the indoor high-tech golf league launched by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy.Rahm was the most high-profile name to join LIV when he left the PGA Tour.Some players, including Brooks Koepka, have since returned to the PGA Tour, which rewrote its rules in December to allow the five-time major winner to come back, subject to certain sanctions.Rahm did not follow suit and remained under long-term contract with LIV, but in May reached a deal with the DP World Tour - formerly the European Tour - to retain his membership and remain eligible for next year's Ryder Cup.LIV golfers are automatically banned for a year by the PGA Tour. The DP World Tour offers a pathway because the leading 10 players on the European circuit currently gain access to PGA Tour membership.In August, former world number one Rahm won his third straight LIV season title.He previously said he had no regrets over joining LIV and backed organisers to make it sustainable.

schema.headline: Jon Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV tour

title: Essex dad sentenced after son died in Cyprus hotel fall
description: A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.Joshua Foster t
body: A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end."Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk.After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened."Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said. He described his client as an "incredible father"."[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.

schema.headline: Essex dad sentenced after son died in Cyprus hotel fall

title: Tiger attack victim's medical records may have been breached
description: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on SaturdayByOliver Wright and Emily JohnsonY
body: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on SaturdayByOliver Wright and Emily JohnsonYorkshireUpdated 5 hours agoMedical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, a spokesperson has said.William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.Image source, Ella FordImage caption, An eyewitness took a photograph of the tiger at the wildlife park shortly before the incidentIn a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives.They said: "We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so."We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits."The trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals. "We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and we will continue to keep William's family informed as our investigation progresses."Image source, Phil Bodmer/BBCImage caption, Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened to visitorsAn inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday heard that Chapman had died of "multiple traumatic injuries".Chapman had attended the park at about 13:30 BST on Saturday, climbed over two fences and entered the tiger enclosure.After the attack, park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended, who confirmed Chapman's death at the scene, the inquest was told.Senior coroner Nicola Mundy said Chapman had a history of mental illness, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had suffered previous bouts of psychosis. The inquest heard that the 24-year-old was under adult mental health services in Doncaster, but was "highly functioning and independent with no care requirements".The self-employed online trader was born in Chichester, West Sussex, and lived in Doncaster at the time of his death.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Tiger attack victim's medical records may have been breached

title: Man City charges: Do Premier League club have grounds for their appeal?
description: Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier Lea
body: Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport.City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating "sham contracts" to inflate sponsorship deals by £830m.The club have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and they have "irrefutable evidence" the ruling "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".In their appeal, City will argue the payments were made by the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder of the sponsors, while there are inconsistencies in the Commission's judgement. Therefore, City say the sponsorship amounts were legitimate and not topped up by the owners.James Severn, Member of the London Solicitor Litigation Association (LSLA) and Partner at Penningtons Manches Cooper, told BBC Sport the appeal is "not simply an opportunity to invite a new panel" to get the verdict overturned."City will need to identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness, which materially affected the Commission's decision," Severn said. "The Appeal Board nevertheless has broad powers to allow or dismiss the appeal, vary the decision or make any other order it considers appropriate."Etihad Airways, one of City's principle sponsors at the centre of the case, had previously stated that the Abu Dhabi government had not paid for its sponsorship of Manchester City.That came in court documents as part of a US investigation in New York in 2015.City will argue this does not have the full context of the situation and is not proof they have been inconsistent with evidence.The club are adamant government documents fully support their case - but, Severn said, if these were already available to the Commission they may not be much use in an appeal."The bank statements, government records and contemporaneous payment documents could be powerful evidence if they establish a clear audit trail showing the disputed funds came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the owners," Severn added. "However, if that evidence was already before the Commission, which nevertheless concluded that the arrangements were a sham, City will face an uphill struggle to demonstrate the finding was materially wrong."Shortly before City's appeal was confirmed, Etihad Airways issued a statement saying it had never been "given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon".Severn said Etihad Airways' complaint "does not, of itself, establish procedural unfairness"."Etihad was not the respondent and is unlikely to have had an independent right to participate in the proceedings," Severn said. "It is likely to have been open to either party to obtain and present such evidence to the Commission. "If the Appeal Board is prepared to consider new evidence from Etihad, it is likely to carry greater weight if supported by contemporaneous documents."A key part of City's defence will be that the Independent Commission relied too heavily on the emails obtained through the Football Leaks files."If City can demonstrate the Commission fundamentally misunderstood the emails, failed to consider their proper context or reached conclusions inconsistent with other contemporaneous documents, that could amount to a material factual error," Severn added. "City's difficulty is that the Commission heard extensive witness and documentary evidence but nevertheless made serious findings of sham arrangements and disguised owner funding."Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport the commission found "the documents were retrofitted to fit the crime". "The Commission must have concluded that the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses put up by Manchester City were poor," Maguire said."However, from a legal point of view, this is an area they could attack if Manchester City's team can prove that the commission itself was a flawed construct in the sense that the members were Premier League picks rather than Manchester City's, and therefore the deck was stacked against the club to begin with. "But that seems remote." Severn added that the retired senior judges and leading barristers, who sat on the Commission, have "spent their careers interpreting complicated facts, dealing with witnesses and applying relevant weight to evidence".While adding that it would be "impossible to assess reliably" the chances of City winning their appeal, Severn added that "doing so will not be easy". But Maguire believes that while it will be difficult for City to be successful, "there is a route".City have brought in Mark Howard KC to advise the club in their appeal, while Etihad Airways has enlisted the services of respected law firm Quinn Emanuel.Maguire said: "Given the lawyers that have been recruited by Manchester City, they may go down what's been described to me as a mess and noise approach."That means trying to discredit everything to do with the process of the Commission rather than necessarily the evidence that was presented. "I've seen the documents that Abu Dhabi presented to the New York case. I'm not a lawyer, but from an accounting point of view, they can be seen in more than one way."Even though Premier League regulations state an appeal must be heard within 12 weeks, or by Christmas Eve, Severn added that "given the scale and complexity of the proceedings, a final outcome may not be known for some time".

schema.headline: Man City charges: Do Premier League club have grounds for their appeal?

title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: England will relish underdog tag against Tonga
description: Underdogs? We like that tag, says England captain WilliamsImage source, SW PixImage caption, George Williams has been a member of England's previous t
body: Underdogs? We like that tag, says England captain WilliamsImage source, SW PixImage caption, George Williams has been a member of England's previous two World Cup squadsBySteve SutcliffeBBC Sport journalistEngland will relish their underdog tag when they take on a powerful Tonga side in their World Cup opener in Perth on Saturday, captain George Williams says.  They defeated the Pacific Islanders 3-0 in a hard-fought Test series at home three years ago - having previously edged to victory in a dramatic World Cup semi-final in Auckland in 2017. But England - who have already suffered a blow with the withdrawal of Morgan Smithies through injury - have been forced into a late change to their starting line-up, with Luke Thompson replacing the absent Morgan Knowles. And with humidity expected to be above 60% inside HBF Park, Williams expects the toughest of starts against a Tonga side who have evolved since 2023 and are packed with NRL talent."Tonga are a stacked team. They have been for a few years now," Williams said."We'll be underdogs but we'll quite like that kind of brush on our head and we'll bring our game tomorrow night against a great team. "I think it's always different over here as well, with the heat and different conditions. It helps when you drag them to Leeds and it's minus two or whatever it normally is in November. "We're looking forward to the challenge. They are stacked full of world-class players who play across the NRL, so we know what we are in for, but we are fully prepared and ready."Rugby League World Cup15 October - 15 NovemberAustralia, Papua New Guinea, New ZealandListen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and appFigure caption, England captain George Williams looks ahead to his third Rugby League World CupEngland's recent World Cup history is one of heartache and near misses. In 2022, they fell to a golden-point loss to Samoa in the last four and in 2017 they were beaten 6-0 by Australia in the final.Williams, 31, who was part of those squads and captain when England lost 3-0 in the Ashes in 2025, dismissed any idea that baggage could inhibit the group now at head coach Brian McDermott's disposal."I don't think it hinders us. Some of the lads were talking about the last World Cup and it was probably one of the most difficult losses of my career to date," Williams added."It does sit there. You can't hide away from what happened but what it can do is give you drive and motivation and there's still numerous players within the group that felt that but the good thing is we've got a mixed bag. "Some youth, some heritage and some old lads like myself can all mingle together and get the job done."England aim to show new attacking verveImage source, SW PixImage caption, Brian McDermott was named England head coach in April, on a deal through to the end of the World CupEngland's toils in the Ashes 12 months ago led to McDermott replacing Shaun Wane at the helm. And it has also brought the promise of a "point of difference" in attack as they prepare for a potentially pivotal first match. With Australia and New Zealand expected to advance from Pool A, it leaves England likely to fight it out with Tonga, Samoa and Papua New Guinea from Pools B and C - which will be combined into one six-team table - for the other two semi-final spots."It's definitely been different. I'm not going to tell you all the tricks and what we're up to and what we're talking about, but it has been different and it's been enjoyable," added the Dolphins-bound Williams, who is keen to impress as he goes up against his his new club head coach Kristian Woolf and future halves partner in Isaiya Katoa."I think the group have all bought into what he wants us to do."Most Test matches start the same way, very physical, and that won't be changing at all this week for any game. "Don't be expecting this mad expansive style of free-for-all but we're going to put some stuff in there that we've not done previously."Figure caption, Explaining the unusual group format of the Men's Rugby League World Cup'I know all their strengths'Image source, SW PixImage caption, Jodie Cunningham will start on the bench against WalesEngland get their Women's World Cup campaign under way directly prior to the men's match, as they take on Wales in a must-win opening game in Perth (07:35 BST). Stuart Barrow's side thrashed the World Cup debutants 62-0 in August 2025 and claimed a record 82-0 win at Headingley over the same opponents in 2024.  However, Wales have strengthened since then, with second rower Paige Travis - who has switched allegiances from England - and Canterbury Bulldogs half-back Tayla Preston lining up for them on Saturday. "I've seen Paige Travis and Dani McGifford and my team-mates at St Helens. I know all their strengths and how fantastic they are," said captain Jodie Cunningham, who has been named on the bench for Saturday's match and is set to appear at a fourth World Cup."Hopefully we come out on top. The combinations are really starting to come together now, so we're just excited and we're all ready to go." England, ranked third in the world, will then take on reigning champions Australia and Samoa as they attempt to reach the last four for a fifth time.

schema.headline: Rugby League World Cup 2026: England will relish underdog tag against Tonga

title: Street Fighter cast say movie 'for the fans' - will they show up?
description: Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie versio
body: Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series.The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987.Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before.But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse.BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same.The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji.The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour.Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison.The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs."It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat."And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game."He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail. Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film.His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look."I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says."My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'". Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far.Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula."I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says."I think we could feel it when we first read the script."Critics, though, haven't been convinced.

schema.headline: Street Fighter cast say movie 'for the fans' - will they show up?

title: Defoe, Solskjaer, Giroud: Ranking the Premier League's greatest super subs
description: ByAlex BysouthBBC Sport senior journalistMikel Arteta may be attempting to rebrand them "finishers" but there's only one phrase in the footballing lex
body: ByAlex BysouthBBC Sport senior journalistMikel Arteta may be attempting to rebrand them "finishers" but there's only one phrase in the footballing lexicon to sum up today's focus: super subs. Yes, we're looking for those players renowned for making a devastating impact off the bench, those guaranteed game-changers a manager turns to when in desperate need of a goal. First, an honorary mention for some who missed out, such as one-season wonder Adam le Fondre, who holds the record for the most goals off the bench in a single Premier League campaign - five of his eight came in a three-game spell in January 2013. Hernan Crespo boasts the best goals-per-game ratio but his six in 16 substitute appearances for Chelsea represents a small sample size, likewise ex-Norwich and Leicester forward Mark Robins with five in 14 outings as a replacement.To make the all-time top 10 Premier League super subs, players need to have consistently delivered throughout their careers, providing goals and assists. So here we go, I've ranked mine below - you can have your say in the comments, too.10. Theo WalcottTheo Walcott, replaced on 168 occasions, holds the record as the most subbed off player in Premier League history. Yet it's his impact coming on to the pitch we're interested in here. Bursting on to the top-flight scene as an explosive teenager, the flying forward was often used by Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger to stretch defences with his pace and movement - a lactic acid-inducing sight for flailing full-backs.The England international pieced together an impressive substitute CV throughout his Premier League career.No-one has more than Walcott's 14 assists as a sub - Ryan Giggs and Marc Albrighton are level - while he also scored 10 goals as a replacement across his time with the Gunners, Everton and Southampton.It puts him fourth on the list for overall goal contributions off the bench.9. Victor AnichebeThis was a toss up between Victor Anichebe and Divock Origi, with both forwards contributing exactly half of all their Premier League goals as a substitute. Ex-Everton, West Brom and Sunderland striker Anichebe edges it having notched a couple more - a tally of 13 placing the former Nigeria international in joint-eighth on the all-time list - while he also chipped in with five assists off the bench.Roman Pavlyuchenko was also unlucky to miss out - 45% of his 20 Premier League goals came as a substitute for Tottenham.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Anichebe scored 50% of his 26 Premier League goals as a sub - the joint-highest percentage for any player to have scored at least 20 times in the competition8. Daniel SturridgeThere's a good case for Danny Welbeck, who as the only current player in the top three, with 19 goals, still has time to catch those above him.Welbeck was a goalscoring sub at Manchester United and Arsenal but perfected the art on the south coast, with 12 of his tally coming during six years with Brighton.The 35-year-old is now at Chelsea but - with apologies to Danny - there is another former Blue whose stats demand a place on this list.Daniel Sturridge has two fewer substitute goals then Welbeck but has scored a slightly higher percentage of his overall Premier League tally as a sub - 22%. The former England man, who played for Manchester City, Chelsea, Bolton, Liverpool and West Brom in the top flight, was good for an assist, too.In fact, when you take his total goal contributions of 24, he provided at a more prolific rate than every substitute in Premier League history - bar Edin Dzeko and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. Richarlison matches Sturridge for minutes per goal contribution, but with eight fewer the Brazilian, perhaps harshly, misses out.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sturridge scored 17 of his 76 Premier League goals as a substitute and also made seven assists off the bench7. Olivier GiroudA World Cup and Champions League winner, one of the few trophies Olivier Giroud hasn't got his hands on is the Premier League title despite a knack for scoring important goals off the bench. The Frenchman is second on the all-time substitute scoring list, accounting for 21 of his 90 top-flight goals - that's almost a quarter - with only Dzeko, Solskjaer and Javier Hernandez boasting a better minutes-per-goal record as a sub.Giroud honed his ability to make a late impact at Arsenal and Chelsea, making 103 substitute appearances in total across 10 seasons in the Premier League.6. Tore Andre FloGood feet for a big man. Tore Andre Flo was a menace for Premier League defenders not merely because of his tall, gangly frame but for the silky touches the Norwegian often showed with his giant boots.Flo scored 34% of his 38 Premier League goals as a substitute - the eighth-highest ratio for those with 20 top-flight goals or more, while he is also joint-eighth overall for goals from a substitute.The first of those came just three minutes into his Chelsea debut in 1997, and it was with the Blues he enjoyed his best Premier League output before a later stint at Sunderland.Having also provided three assists as a sub, he ranks fifth for minutes-per-goal involvements, contributing to his side scoring once every 78 minutes on average when used off the bench.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Twelve of Flo's 34 Premier League goals for Chelsea came as a substitute 5. Javier HernandezThe Little Pea. Small in stature but a giant headache for tiring defenders.Of all players in Premier League history to have scored at least 10 goals as a substitute, only one - Sergio Aguero, and it feels a stretch to call the competition's sixth-highest scorer a super sub - has netted at a more prolific rate than Javier 'Chicharito' Hernandez.He has 19 in 78 sub appearances, a rate of 0.24 per game, with 36% of all his Premier League goals coming after he started on the bench - predominantly for Manchester United but also later in his career at West Ham. He netted on average every 88 minutes when used as a replacement.Indeed, only Jermain Defoe and Giroud have scored more goals as a substitute than the Mexican, while he sits among a leading group of seven - including Defoe - who have scored five match-winners as a sub. 4. Edin DzekoAged 40, Edin Dzeko is still scoring goals for Bundesliga outfit Schalke. His record as a substitute in the Premier League, however, remains among the greatest.Dzeko netted 50 Premier League goals for Manchester City, with more than a quarter of those coming as a substitute. Only Aguero and Hernandez, of players to have scored at least 10 goals as a sub, have better goals-per-game ratios than him. When you break it down to minutes per goal, Dzeko is level at the top with Solskjaer - scoring on average every 83 minutes.He stands alone once you add assists, too - 17 goal contributions during 56 top-flight games as a replacement means Dzeko returned on average every 63 minutes. The most important of those goals, of course, came in stoppage time against QPR on the final day of the 2012 season. Everyone remembers the Aguero moment, but it was substitute Dzeko's header two minutes earlier that levelled the game.3. Ole Gunnar SolskjaerOle Gunnar Solskjaer is perhaps the most iconic of super subs, largely for that Treble-clinching night in Barcelona.The baby-faced Norwegian, having started Manchester United's FA Cup final win over Newcastle four days earlier, came on in the 81st minute of the Champions League final to toe-poke a stoppage-time winner after Teddy Sheringham had equalised against Bayern Munich moments earlier.It capped a vintage few months for Solskjaer's super sub legend, having bagged four in the final 10 minutes of an 8-1 win at Nottingham Forest in the February.Sticking strictly to his Premier League output, Solskjaer is joint-fifth on the all-time substitute scoring list with 17, netting 19% of his 91 top-flight goals off the bench, with a ratio of 0.2 goals-per-game as a sub.His rate of scoring on average once every 83 minutes off the bench is a competition high that can only be matched by Dzeko. The caveat is, like Dzeko, Solskjaer was playing for one of the most dominant teams in the land.2. Nwankwo KanuNwankwo Kanu's impact as a substitute was felt immediately at Arsenal.Coming off the bench on his debut, the Nigerian forward collected a throw-in meant for a Sheffield United player - after the opposition kicked the ball out for an injury - and crossed for Marc Overmars to score. It sparked a famous FA Cup rematch. In the Premier League, he was just as ruthless. Kanu, who joined from Inter Milan having earlier won the Champions League at Ajax, made 56 of his 119 top-flight appearances for Arsenal as a sub.When you take in spells at West Brom and Portsmouth, too, he netted 17 goals off the bench - 31% of all his top-flight strikes - which places him joint-fifth on the all-time substitute scoring list.But he was almost as prolific at creating them, making 12 assists as a substitute - a tally only bettered by three players in Premier League history.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kanu made 119 Premier League appearances in six years at Arsenal1. Jermain DefoeOK, goals are currency and Jermain Defoe has netted more as a substitute than any other Premier League player. Remarkably, the 24 he scored when coming on all came in different fixtures - which, of course, means he has also scored in more games as a substitute than anyone else. And, as mentioned, a league-high five of those were match-winners.He scored six times as a substitute in his debut Premier League season, earning West Ham a 3-2 win at Ipswich with his first top-flight goal, and netted for the final time in the competition 17 years later after coming on to rescue Bournemouth a stoppage-time point at Watford.Simply put, throughout his career, Defoe - also England's highest-scoring substitute with seven goals - was the ruthless finisher a manager wished to see when anxiously glancing at their bench in need of a goal.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Defoe scored a Premier League record 24 goals as a substitute
